description:
​We are a brother-and-sister duo from Tajikistan building a comprehensive health-tracking application to help astronauts monitor their physiological states, track crew well-being, and prevent critical medical situations in space.

​Our Vision:
We hope our application will deliver immense value and serve as a reliable digital companion for the heroes of humanity who are exploring the universe.
summary: AURA (Astronaut Universal Readiness Assessment) is an offline-first web app that lets astronauts assess their own health on long missions, when an answer from the flight surgeon on Earth takes up to 44 minutes round trip — or does not come at all during a solar conjunction. Crew members log vital signs and a short daily check-in, or let onboard sensors send them. AURA checks 15 indicators against their limits, rolls them up into seven body systems and a 0–100 Readiness Score, and turns every result into an explained recommendation: what to do, the numbers behind it, which medical-kit item to use, and when to report to the flight surgeon, with the signal delay stated. It also reads the cabin environment, so a CO₂ problem in a module is linked to the crew’s headaches and poor sleep. Every indicator is tied to NASA Human Research Program hazards and risks, cabin limits come from NASA-STD-3001, and the interface follows NASA’s display standard for crew software. On Mars the crew is its own first responder — AURA makes that safer.
details:
What it does

AURA is a health self-assessment tool for a crew far from Earth. It runs in a browser on a crew laptop or tablet. After sign-in (a password or a passkey — Windows Hello, Touch ID, Face ID) each person sees what their role allows:

  1. Readiness — a 0–100 Readiness Score with its alert class, the active recommendations, today’s tasks and a tile per body system. A value outside its limits carries a coloured ↑/↓ arrow.
  2. Body map — a schematic of seven body systems, each coloured by status. Selecting one shows its readings with nominal (or personal) ranges, how to measure them, why they matter in space, the related NASA HRP risks, countermeasures and what to do.
  3. Log — vitals, a daily check-in (sleep, mood, stress, headache, exercise, water), the personal dosimeter and weekly checks (body mass, vision), with measuring instructions, input validation and a live status preview.
  4. Trends — any indicator over 7, 14 or 30 days, with limit lines, mission phases and spacewalks.
  5. Report — what the flight surgeon receives: summary, out-of-range readings, recommendations with their basis, the cabin air of the member’s module and 7-day trends; downloadable as plain text (for a narrow downlink) or JSON.
  6. Crew (commander, deputy, flight surgeon) — every member’s readiness, all alerts across the crew and 7-day readings side by side.
  7. Vehicle — life support per module (cabin pressure, O₂, CO₂, temperature, humidity, radiation dose rate) with the same alert classes; an off-nominal module produces advice for everyone in it.
  8. Med supplies — the medical kit: stock, location, expiry, a forecast to the end of the mission, inventory counts and a journal. Recommendations point to the item they need.
  9. Profile — the flight surgeon records known conditions, preflight baselines, personal ranges and personal weights for each crew member.

A status bar is always visible: Mission Elapsed Time, UTC, warning and caution counts, link status and the one-way signal delay to Earth.

How it works

  • Indicator catalog: 15 indicators, each with units, a physiologically possible input range, thresholds, measuring instructions, a “why it matters in space” text and links to NASA HRP hazards and risks. Every threshold carries its source.
  • Assessment: each fresh reading is classed Nominal, Caution or Warning; a reading older than its freshness window becomes Stale. A body system takes the worst status of its indicators. The Readiness Score averages the systems (Nominal 100, Caution 60, Warning 20), and any Warning caps it at 49, so one critical value is never hidden by good averages.
  • Explainable guidance: deterministic rules — no black-box model — turn the assessment into actions: sleep debt over several nights, low mood or high stress over several days, low blood oxygen after a spacewalk (hypoxia / decompression risk), repeated critical readings, a slow trend toward a limit while still in range, and cabin air out of limits in the member’s module. Every recommendation states its basis with the actual numbers, when to re-measure, the med-kit item, and — when needed — “report to the flight surgeon”, with the round-trip delay.
  • Personal ranges: the flight surgeon can set individual ranges (for example an athlete’s low resting heart rate) and system weights; the score, rules, report and charts use them.
  • Roles, checked on the server: a crew member sees only their own data; the commander, the deputy and the flight surgeon see the whole crew; readings are logged only by the member themself. Passwords are hashed with PBKDF2-SHA256; passkeys use WebAuthn.
  • Onboard systems: environment sensors, dosimeters and wearables push readings to a token-protected ingest API, documented with OpenAPI and an embedded Swagger UI.
  • Offline-first: one Go binary with an embedded SQLite database serves both the API and the interface. Nothing is loaded from the internet at runtime, so the same build can run on a spacecraft network with no link to Earth.
  • Demo mission: a synthetic 30-day dataset for a crewed Mars expedition (end of transit, landing, surface operations at 0.38 g with spacewalks). No real personal health data is used.

NASA data at the core

The 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight (NASA HRP) classify every indicator, and the HRP Risks of Human Spaceflight link each body system to its official risks and countermeasures. NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 gives the cabin limits — ppCO₂ ≤ 3 mmHg [V2 6004], total pressure [V2 6006], temperature 18–27 °C and humidity 25–75 % [V2 6012] — so habitat telemetry is classed exactly like health data. Curiosity’s RAD measurements (about 0.48 mGy/day in transit, 0.21 mGy/day on Mars) make the dosimeter data realistic, and CSA’s radiation-monitoring work gave the daily dosimeter routine.

Benefits

Autonomy far from Earth with clear, explainable guidance; early warning for slow problems (sleep debt, blood-pressure drift, body-mass loss); health and habitat in one picture, so the fix reaches the cause; built-in education on how to measure and why it matters; and a concise report that fits a narrow, delayed downlink.

Intended impact

For exploration crews — Mars, the Moon, long ISS stays — AURA is a step toward medical autonomy. On Earth the same offline approach fits Antarctic and analog stations, ships, and mountain and rural clinics. Next steps: connect real wearables and life-support telemetry, validate the rules with flight surgeons, and field-test at an analog station.

How it is creative

A readiness model instead of a plain vitals dashboard; delay-aware escalation that says when Earth can answer; physiology and life-support telemetry in one alert language. Our first concept was a bright, gamified app; we dropped it after reading NASA’s display standard for crew software (NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2, Appendix F), because decoration costs a tired astronaut attention. Creativity moved from decoration to the engineering of empathy, and the story is told by our mascot Star Boy, a crew member on Mars.

Factors we considered

Safety and explainability; working with no connection; privacy (server-side roles, passkeys, no real health data); readability under stress (NASA colour meanings, colour never alone, contrast ≥ 6:1); crew time; and honesty — vital-sign thresholds are illustrative clinical references, and AURA is a prototype, not a medical device.

Tools, languages and software

Go 1.26, SQLite (modernc.org/sqlite), OpenAPI 3.1 and Swagger UI; TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, React Router, Recharts; Vitest and oxlint; Docker, Render, GitHub. The Star Boy mascot was drawn in ibisPaint and refined with Google Gemini; the code, documentation and pitch deck were made with the help of Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team. No special hardware is needed — any laptop or tablet with a modern browser.
